w:r.w:t: CAPT-UniShape: Condition-Aware Prototype Transport UniShape for PEMFC Fault Classification
CAPT-UniShape integrates operation, impedance-shape, and condition inputs.
Residual KAN-Fusion enables condition-gated nonlinear multi-source fusion.
Condition-aware RBF prototypes adapt class anchors to operating conditions.
CAPT-UniShape reaches 100.00% Accuracy and Macro-F1 at 8:2 and 7:3.
CAPT-UniShape remains best across four splits and clean-to-10 dB SNR tests.

Reliable fault classification is critical for proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) systems, where water-management faults and operating-condition drift can produce overlapping operation and impedance signatures. This paper presents CAPT-UniShape, a Condition-Aware Prototype Transport UniShape framework that jointly uses six-channel stack-operation windows, constructed EIS-derived impedance-shape sequences, and condition-statistical vectors. Two UniShape backbones encode the operation and impedance-shape inputs, a condition encoder represents the operating regime, Residual KAN-Fusion performs condition-gated multi-source fusion, and an RBF prototype head adapts class anchors to the encoded condition before cosine classification. Unlike a static prototype classifier, the proposed head transports each class prototype along a smooth condition-dependent manifold, allowing the decision geometry to change with operating state. The dataset was obtained from controlled PEMFC stack fault experiments: raw operating, cell-voltage, and EIS-derived variables were recorded in tabular form, converted into segment-level windows, and split into grouped train-validation-test protocols. CAPT-UniShape achieves 98.36% Accuracy and 97.38% Macro-F1 under the 6:4 protocol and 93.46% Accuracy and 89.64% Macro-F1 under the more data-limited 5:5 protocol. In the 6:4 SNR robustness test, performance remains no lower than 96.72% Accuracy and 94.44% Macro-F1 from clean evaluation to 10
These results indicate that the three-input formulation improves class-balanced PEMFC fault classification while keeping the role of operating condition explicit.

w:r.w:t: Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) are a promising option for transportation, distributed generation, and portable energy systems because they offer high conversion efficiency, fast dynamic response, and low local emissions. However, their long-term reliability depends on tightly coupled electrochemical, thermal, water-management, and gas-transport processes. When operating conditions drift beyond the design envelope, the stack may enter membrane dehydration, water flooding, or reactant-starvation states. Each state alters both the macroscopic operating trajectory and the impedance-related response. Accurate PEMFC fault classification is therefore essential for online monitoring, control intervention, and predictive maintenance.

PEMFC fault classification remains difficult because fault signatures are shaped by both internal failure mechanisms and external operating conditions. First, the same physical fault may produce different observable patterns under different load, humidity, pressure, and temperature conditions, whereas benign operating drift may resemble early-stage faults. Second, stack-operation windows and impedance-derived shape sequences describe complementary aspects of the system. Operation variables capture macroscopic dynamic behavior, whereas impedance statistics retain information related to ohmic, charge-transfer, and mass-transport processes. Third, measured PEMFC datasets are usually limited and imbalanced, so a model may appear accurate while still failing to classify minority operating states reliably.

These challenges reveal a gap in common data-driven diagnosis pipelines. Classical classifiers can be efficient, but they usually rely on fixed feature vectors and static decision boundaries. Deep sequence models can learn temporal patterns, but a single operation stream cannot fully represent the electrochemical state of the stack. Multi-source models can integrate richer information, but their fusion strategy must respect the distinct roles of operation windows, impedance-shape responses, and condition variables. A useful PEMFC diagnostic model should therefore preserve input structure, represent operating-condition information explicitly, and remain interpretable enough to explain why the decision boundary changes across conditions.

A second practical gap is that many diagnostic models report high aggregate accuracy without making the source of class separation explicit. In PEMFC fault diagnosis, this is risky because water flooding and membrane dehydration may both appear as changes in voltage stability, impedance response, and thermal-pressure operating state. A useful diagnostic model should therefore preserve time-series morphology, retain impedance-related physical cues, and reveal how changes in operating conditions reshape the decision boundary.

To address this gap, this paper proposes CAPT-UniShape, a three-input PEMFC fault-classification framework. CAPT-UniShape uses two official UniShape backbones to encode six-channel stack-operation windows and constructed EIS-derived impedance-shape sequences. It also uses a condition encoder to embed the 7-dimensional condition-statistical vector, a Residual KAN-Fusion module for multi-source representation fusion, and a condition-aware RBF prototype transport head for cosine prototype classification. The overall workflow is shown in Fig. 1, and the dynamic prototype classifier is detailed in Fig. 4. This design keeps the operation, impedance-shape, and condition streams separate until representation fusion. It then allows the condition token to influence both the fused feature and the prototype geometry.

The empirical study is organized around three questions. The main comparison asks whether the full framework outperforms classical machine-learning, convolutional, and Transformer-style baselines under the same split protocols. The ablation study asks which design choices remain useful under clean, low-noise, and high-noise settings. The robustness study asks whether the proposed model remains stable when joint test-time perturbations are applied to the three inputs. All reported internal-benchmark results are derived from the controlled PEMFC stack fault experiments described in Section 4.1. Therefore, claims about generalization beyond this experimental source are reserved for future validation rather than presented as established evidence.

The scope of this work is correspondingly bounded. CAPT-UniShape is not presented as a new electrochemical mechanism model or as a closed-loop control strategy. Instead, it is designed as a fault-classification framework for controlled PEMFC fault-test data, with emphasis on multi-source representation, condition-aware classification, and protocol-separated validation.
The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows.

First, we formulate PEMFC fault classification as a three-input problem that jointly uses six-channel stack-operation windows, constructed EIS-derived impedance-shape sequences, and condition-statistical vectors. This formulation preserves their structural roles instead of collapsing them into a single flat feature vector.

Second, we design a Residual KAN-Fusion module that combines a stable MLP path with a bottleneck KAN residual path under condition-driven gating. We evaluate its contribution under clean, 30 dB, and 5 dB conditions rather than assuming a uniform gain across all protocols.

Third, we propose a condition-aware RBF prototype transport head (CAPT) that adapts static class prototypes to the encoded operating condition through smooth RBF mapping. This design yields a condition-sensitive prototype classifier whose empirical benefit is reported with explicit protocol boundaries.

Finally, we validate the framework on a measured PEMFC dataset across the 8:2, 7:3, 6:4, and 5:5 protocols. We further evaluate robustness under a 6:4, seed-44, test-only SNR protocol and use a 6:4 three-scenario ablation to separate clean, 30 dB, and 5 dB behavior.

This section reviews four research directions that motivate CAPT-UniShape: PEMFC fault diagnosis, time-series shape representation, multi-modal and condition-aware learning, and prototype learning with KAN-based nonlinear modeling. Rather than providing an
exhaustive survey, we focus on the limitations that remain most relevant to condition-dependent PEMFC diagnosis.

PEMFC fault diagnosis has been studied through model-based observers, signal-processing features, traditional machine-learning methods, and deep neural networks. Model-based approaches are useful when stack dynamics and fault mechanisms can be described with sufficient fidelity, but practical stacks often operate under varying load, water content, and thermal conditions. Data-driven methods reduce the need for explicit physical modeling, yet the diagnostic value they retain depends strongly on the chosen input representation. Voltage- and current-based features are easy to deploy, but they are highly load-dependent and may be insensitive to early electrochemical changes. By contrast, EIS is more directly linked to internal electrochemical processes and distinguishes ohmic, charge-transfer, and mass-transport regions, which makes it attractive for diagnosing water-management and starvation faults.

A limitation particularly relevant to this study is that operation signals, EIS-derived statistics, and operating-condition variables are often handled either as independent diagnostic views or as a single concatenated feature vector. This treatment can obscure the structural relationships among impedance statistics and conceal the condition dependence of the decision boundary. CAPT-UniShape addresses this issue by constructing a four-channel impedance-shape sequence, preserving a separate operation branch, and using the condition vector in both feature fusion and prototype transport. This distinction is architectural, not merely an expansion of the input feature set.

For laboratory PEMFC datasets, this limitation is further compounded by class imbalance and by the fact that fault labels are usually assigned to operating episodes rather than isolated time points. Methods that ignore segment structure may learn shortcuts from dominant operating regions, whereas methods that rely only on aggregate impedance indicators may miss transient information contained in the stack-operation sequence. Accordingly, the present work treats operation windows, impedance-derived shape descriptors, and condition variables as separate yet coupled sources of diagnostic evidence.

Deep learning models for time-series classification include convolutional networks, recurrent networks, Transformers, and more recent foundation-style time-series backbones. These models are relevant to PEMFC diagnosis because faults may manifest through local trends, response curvature, transient changes, and multi-scale temporal patterns. However, generic sequence encoders usually assume that each input stream can be treated as a homogeneous time series. PEMFC diagnosis does not fully satisfy this assumption, because operation windows, impedance statistics, and condition variables carry different semantics and should not be forced into a common representation before their roles are established.

Shape-aware representation therefore provides a useful intermediate perspective. UniShape, which is adopted here as the official backbone for operation and EIS-derived impedance-shape encoding, provides transferable shape embeddings across heterogeneous time-series inputs. This study does not modify the UniShape backbone itself. Instead, it adapts two UniShape encoders to the PEMFC setting and places them within a condition-aware multi-input architecture, in which the operation and EIS-derived impedance branches remain distinct until fusion.

In fault diagnosis, shape representation is especially useful when the absolute magnitude of a signal changes with load, temperature, or pressure, but its relative profile still carries diagnostic information. The constructed impedance-shape branch in this work follows this principle: ordered impedance statistics are not treated solely as an unordered feature vector, but are interpolated into a compact multi-channel sequence so that slope, cumulative deviation, and relative position can be encoded by a time-series backbone.

Multi-modal fault diagnosis typically combines sensor streams, handcrafted features, and contextual variables through early fusion, late fusion, attention, or gating mechanisms. Early fusion is simple, but it can blur the boundary between physically distinct signal types. Late fusion preserves modality-specific decisions, but it may miss interactions that emerge only after joint representation learning. Attention and gating offer an intermediate strategy, but they still require a clear definition of the contribution of each modality. In PEMFC diagnosis, condition variables are not merely auxiliary metadata. They define the operating envelope within which a fault signature is observed.

CAPT-UniShape therefore treats the condition vector as both a source of representation and a driver of decision geometry. In the fusion module, the condition token helps rebalance the operation and impedance-shape representations. In the classification head, the same condition information is mapped to prototype offsets, allowing class anchors to move smoothly with the operating state. This design explicitly links operating context to both feature fusion and class geometry.

Condition-aware learning also helps distinguish fault evidence from operating-regime evidence. In a PEMFC stack, the same voltage or impedance pattern can have different meanings under different gas-supply, temperature, or pressure states. This motivates the use of condition-driven gates in the fusion stage and condition-dependent prototype displacement in the classifier, rather than treating the condition vector as just another concatenated feature.

Prototype-based classification represents each class with one or more reference vectors and assigns samples according to their similarity to those vectors. This is appealing for fault diagnosis because the learned decision rule can be interpreted geometrically: a sample is assigned to the class whose prototype is most similar to its fused representation. Static prototypes, however, can become restrictive when class distributions shift across operating conditions. RBF mappings provide smooth local interpolation from condition space to prototype displacement, which is well suited to condition-dependent yet continuous adaptation of the decision boundary.

KAN layers provide another mechanism for introducing controlled nonlinearity through basis expansions. In this work, KAN is not used as a standalone classifier. Instead, it is placed behind a bottleneck and added as a residual branch to an MLP fusion path. This design is intentionally conservative because the dataset is limited and the method should not rely on an unconstrained high-capacity fusion block. Accordingly, the module-level interpretation is treated as protocol-specific evidence rather than as proof that each module yields an independent gain in every setting.

The combined use of prototypes and KAN-style residual mapping is therefore deliberately conservative. Prototype learning provides an interpretable class-anchor geometry, whereas the KAN branch contributes a limited nonlinear correction within the fusion block. The ablation results are interpreted within this boundary: these modules are evaluated as
components that may improve condition sensitivity and robustness under specific protocols, rather than as independently optimal choices in every test scenario.

The EIS-derived input is a constructed impedance-statistical shape sequence built from nine ordered impedance statistics obtained from EIS-related measurements: total impedance, mean impedance, maximum impedance, second-highest impedance, minimum impedance, second-lowest impedance, standard deviation, EIS resistance real part, and EIS resistance imaginary part. The ordered vector is interpolated onto 128 normalized positions to obtain c_i. The first-difference channel g_i is computed along this interpolated curve, the cumulative-shape channel a_i is obtained by cumulatively summing the mean-centered curve, and q is the normalized coordinate channel. The resulting four-channel sequence is defined in Eq. (2).

a_i is the centered cumulative shape;
q is the normalized coordinate channel.

This four-step construction can be read as interpolation, first difference, centered cumulative shape, and coordinate augmentation. All four channels are normalized with training-partition statistics before model input.

This construction, summarized in Fig. 2, supplies a shape-like interface for the UniShape encoder while preserving the relative geometry of the underlying impedance statistics. Together with the six-channel length-256 operation window and the 7-dimensional condition vector, it defines the three input streams used by CAPT-UniShape.

The model follows a three-branch representation design (Fig. 1). The operation sequence and the constructed EIS-derived impedance-shape sequence are encoded by two official UniShape backbone wrappers that share structure but not weights. The condition embedding serves as both a feature source in the fusion module and the driver of condition-dependent prototype displacement in the classification head, so that operating conditions can influence the feature distribution as well as the class decision geometry.

The EIS-derived branch receives a constructed four-channel sequence rather than a raw scalar feature vector; the construction procedure is shown in Fig. 2. This keeps the ordered impedance-statistical profile visible to the UniShape encoder.

Before Residual KAN-Fusion, the encoded condition token generates two sigmoid gates, one for the operation branch and one for the EIS-derived branch. As shown in Fig. 3, the gated branch features are added to the condition embedding to form the fusion input, which is then mapped through a stable MLP path and a bottleneck KAN residual path:

u_i is the condition-gated fusion input;
lambda_KAN is the learnable KAN residual scale;

The MLP branch carries the main fusion path. The KAN branch first compresses the concatenated representation through a bottleneck, applies a KAN-style nonlinear transformation that expands normalized scalar inputs on learnable Gaussian basis functions, and then projects the output back to the fused representation dimension. FiLM-style modulation from the condition token injects condition information inside the fusion module. KAN regularization penalizes basis-weight scale and center spacing, keeping this branch as a controlled nonlinear residual rather than an independent classifier.

Compared with a purely static prototype head, this formulation allows each class anchor to move along a smooth, condition-dependent manifold while preserving the geometric interpretation of prototype-based classification. Because the latest ablation shows protocol-dependent behavior, this mechanism is claimed as a condition-aware design rather than as a universally superior variant in every noise setting.

This section describes the laboratory PEMFC dataset collected from controlled stack fault experiments, preprocessing pipeline, split protocols, training configuration, baseline models, and evaluation metrics used to compare diagnostic performance.
The dataset used in this study was obtained from controlled PEMFC stack fault experiments. During the experiments, stack operation, single-cell voltage, and EIS-derived

impedance variables were recorded into a raw Excel table before conversion into NPZ archives for the official model pipeline. The raw table contains 11,137 rows and 230 columns, including test time, numeric label, 216 single-cell voltage columns, stack total voltage, stack total current, stack power, and nine EIS-derived impedance statistics. The row-level label counts are 1,752 for class 0, 2,036 for class 1, and 7,349 for class 2. After segment-based windowing, the evaluated dataset contains 433 windows distributed as 74, 68, and 291 across classes 0, 1, and 2. Because the dataset comes from a controlled laboratory fault-test source and has not been publicly released, all reported results should be interpreted as internal benchmarks; generalization to external datasets is a stated direction for future work.

The baselines cover three families: classical machine learning (logistic regression, SVM, random forest), feed-forward and convolutional networks (MLP, 1D-CNN), and Transformer-style backbones (Transformer, iTransformer). All baselines are trained and evaluated on the same seed-44 split protocol as the proposed model for each train-test ratio, and the SNR robustness comparison uses the same 6:4 noise protocol as the proposed model.

Classical models such as logistic regression, SVM, and random forest degrade more strongly after perturbation, whereas MLP and Transformer-family models remain more stable but start from a lower clean baseline.

The SNR experiment should be interpreted as a unified noise-sensitivity comparison within the 6:4, seed-44, test-only protocol. It should not be directly cross-tabulated with the 8:2 clean result, the four-ratio comparison, or the three-scenario ablation, because those experiments use different checkpoints, noise seeds, scripts, or evaluation protocols. Within this boundary, the SNR evidence supports the claim that CAPT-UniShape is both the strongest clean classifier and the most stable model across the tested SNR range.

CAPT-UniShape delivers the best test performance across the 8:2, 7:3, 6:4, and 5:5 protocols, with the advantage especially clear for Macro-F1. This indicates that the framework improves class-balanced behavior rather than only exploiting the dominant Flooding or over-wet class. The three-scenario ablation shows a more nuanced mechanism picture: condition input is important, the full model is not the best variant at 30 dB, and the complete RBF-based design is strongest under 5 dB high noise together with static prototypes. Three limitations should be noted. First, the current conclusions are based on seed-44 split protocols. This means that the reported margins may include split-specific variance, especially for minority classes with fewer windows; a direct next step is to repeat the four-ratio comparison, ablation, and SNR tests across multiple random seeds and report mean, standard deviation, and confidence intervals. Second, the dataset was collected from one controlled experimental source. This supports controlled internal benchmarking but does not establish deployment generalization across stacks, laboratories, sensor configurations, or fault-induction procedures; future work should evaluate the same pipeline on external PEMFC datasets and, where possible, cross-stack transfer protocols. Third, the four-ratio comparison, the three-scenario ablation, and the SNR robustness comparison use related but non-identical protocols, so their clean rows and noisy rows should not be mixed as if they came from one factorial experiment. A fully crossed experiment using the same checkpoint-selection rule, noise seeds, and split protocol would be needed to isolate all interaction effects among data ratio, noise level, and architectural module. This paper introduces CAPT-UniShape, a condition-aware prototype transport framework for PEMFC fault classification that ingests six-channel stack-operation windows, constructed EIS-derived impedance-shape sequences, and condition-statistical vectors in parallel. The architecture combines two official UniShape backbones, an MLP condition encoder, Residual KAN-Fusion with condition-driven gating, and a condition-aware RBF prototype transport head. On the current seed-44 laboratory PEMFC dataset collected from controlled stack fault experiments, CAPT-UniShape achieves the best result across the 8:2, 7:3, 6:4, and 5:5 protocols, reaching 100.00% Accuracy and 100.00% Macro-F1 at 8:2 and 7:3, 98.36% Accuracy and 97.38% Macro-F1 at 6:4, and 93.46% Accuracy and 89.64% Macro-F1 at 5:5. The SNR robustness results show that CAPT-UniShape maintains at least 96.72% Accuracy and 94.44% Macro-F1 from clean to 10
